title: What is RDS, and how is it different from running a database yourself on EC2 (managed backups, patching, Multi-AZ failover, read replicas)?
shortTitle: RDS and How It Differs From Running a Database Yourself on EC2
keyPoints: RDS is a managed relational database where AWS handles provisioning, backups, patching, failover, and replication.
Automated backups take daily snapshots and continuous transaction logs, enabling point-in-time recovery to any second.
Engine and OS patching is applied automatically during a maintenance window you choose.
Multi-AZ keeps a synchronous standby in another AZ and fails over automatically in about one to two minutes.
Read replicas are asynchronous copies for offloading read-heavy reporting from the primary instance.
Running a database on EC2 gives full OS and engine control but requires you to manage backups, patching, failover, and replication manually.
RDS trades some control for reliability and reduced operational burden, which is usually the right trade for banking workloads.

s1_definition.oneliner: RDS is a managed relational database where AWS does backups, patching, failover, and replication for you, while a database on EC2 means you do all of that operational work yourself.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **RDS (Relational Database Service)** – A managed service that runs relational database engines (PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server) with automated operational tasks.
- **Automated Backups** – Daily snapshots and continuous transaction log capture, enabling point-in-time recovery to any second within the retention window.
- **Multi-AZ** – A synchronous standby replica in another Availability Zone with automatic failover, providing high availability with no code changes.
- **Read Replicas** – Asynchronous copies of the primary that offload read-only queries, scalable within the same or other Regions.
- **Database on EC2** – A self-managed database installed on a virtual machine where you control everything but own all the operational burden.
s1_definition.analogy: Running a database on EC2 is like buying an empty building and doing everything yourself at National Bank of India: install the vault door, hire guards, arrange nightly backups to another location, patch the locks when a flaw is found, and if the building burns down, scramble to rebuild. RDS is like renting a fully managed vault from a specialist security firm: they install and maintain the door, take nightly backups automatically, patch the locks on schedule, keep a mirror vault in another building that takes over instantly if the first fails, and give you extra reading rooms so many clerks can read ledgers at once.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Amazon RDS is a managed relational database service. I pick an engine like PostgreSQL, an instance size, and storage, and AWS takes over the operational heavy lifting – provisioning, backups, patching, failover, and replication. The whole point is that it removes the undifferentiated work of running a database so my team can focus on schema and queries instead of operations.

The concrete differences from running a database myself on EC2 come down to four things. Automated backups: RDS takes daily snapshots and continuously captures transaction logs, giving me point-in-time recovery to any second in the retention window, whereas on EC2 I would script and test all of that myself. Patching: RDS applies engine and operating-system patches in a maintenance window I choose, whereas on EC2 I track and apply every patch by hand. Multi-AZ: RDS keeps a synchronous standby in another Availability Zone and fails over to it automatically in about ninety seconds, whereas on EC2 I would build my own replication and failover. And read replicas: RDS gives me asynchronous read-only copies to offload heavy reporting from the primary.

The trade-off, and the senior point I always raise, is control. With RDS I do not get operating-system shell access, I am limited to supported engine versions and the parameters exposed through parameter groups, and a very specialized or unsupported configuration can force me onto EC2. For the vast majority of banking workloads that lost control is well worth the reliability and reduced operational burden.

At National Bank of India I ran the core ledger on RDS PostgreSQL with Multi-AZ enabled. When an Availability Zone had an outage, RDS automatically promoted the synchronous standby and repointed the endpoint, and our transfer service reconnected within about ninety seconds with no code change and no data loss. I used read replicas for month-end reports and let RDS handle patching in a quiet maintenance window. Doing all of that manually on EC2 would have meant a full operations team and far more risk.

Remember one sentence: RDS does backups, patching, Multi-AZ failover, and read replicas for you, while a database on EC2 means you own all of that operational work yourself.
